     2→title: Ray.Toolkit.Automerge
     3→description: Production-ready C# bindings for building collaborative applications with conflict-free data structures
     4→---
     5→
     6→# Overview
     7→
     8→Ray.Toolkit.Automerge provides C# bindings for the Automerge library, which implements Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs).
     9→
    10→CRDTs let multiple users edit the same data simultaneously without conflicts. When changes merge, the system automatically resolves conflicts in predictable ways. This means you can build collaborative applications where users work offline and sync later.
    11→
    12→The library wraps a Rust-based implementation, giving you high performance with a clean C# API.
    13→
    14→# What You Can Build
    15→
    16→This library works well for applications where multiple users modify shared data:
    17→
    18→- Collaborative document editors
    19→- Real-time task management systems
    20→- Distributed configuration systems
    21→- Offline-first mobile applications
    22→- Multi-user data synchronization
    23→
    24→# Key Capabilities
    25→
    26→**Automatic Conflict Resolution**
    27→
    28→Multiple users can edit the same document at the same time. The library merges changes automatically without requiring manual conflict resolution.
    29→
    30→**Offline Support**
    31→
    32→Users can work completely offline. Changes sync and merge when connectivity returns.
    33→
    34→**Complete History**
    35→
    36→Every change is tracked with commit history. You can inspect what changed, when, and by whom.
    37→
    38→**Efficient Synchronization**
    39→
    40→The sync protocol exchanges only the differences between documents, minimizing network traffic.
    41→
    42→**Type-Safe API**
    43→
    44→The C# API provides type safety and follows .NET conventions, making it feel natural to .NET developers.
    45→
    46→# Quick Example
    47→
    48→Here's a minimal example showing document creation and synchronization between two peers:
    49→
    50→```csharp
    51→using Ray.Toolkit.Automerge;
    52→
    53→// Alice creates a document
    54→using var alice = AutomergeDocument.Create();
    55→var root = alice.RootId;
    56→
    57→alice.PutString(root, "title", "Meeting Notes");
    58→alice.PutBoolean(root, "published", false);
    59→alice.Commit("Initial draft");
    60→
    61→// Bob creates his own document
    62→using var bob = AutomergeDocument.Create();
    63→var bobRoot = bob.RootId;
    64→bob.PutString(bobRoot, "author", "Bob");
    65→bob.Commit("Add author");
    66→
    67→// Sync the documents
    68→using var aliceSync = alice.CreateSyncState();
    69→using var bobSync = bob.CreateSyncState();
    70→
    71→var msg1 = alice.GenerateSyncMessage(aliceSync);
    72→if (msg1 != null) bob.ReceiveSyncMessage(bobSync, msg1);
    73→
    74→var msg2 = bob.GenerateSyncMessage(bobSync);
    75→if (msg2 != null) alice.ReceiveSyncMessage(aliceSync, msg2);
    76→
    77→// Both documents now contain all changes
    78→// alice has: title, published, author
    79→// bob has: title, published, author
    80→```
    81→
    82→# How It Works
    83→
    84→Automerge uses CRDTs to track changes at a fine-grained level. Each modification gets a unique identifier based on the actor (user) and a logical timestamp.
    85→
    86→When you merge documents, Automerge looks at these identifiers to determine the order of operations. It applies mathematical rules to combine changes, ensuring all peers converge to the same state.
    87→
    88→This approach differs from traditional operational transformation or manual conflict resolution. You don't need to write conflict handlers or choose between competing changes.
    89→
    90→# Architecture
    91→
    92→The library consists of two main packages:
    93→
    94→**Ray.Toolkit.Automerge**
    95→
    96→The high-level API you'll use in your applications. It provides managed types and .NET-friendly methods.
    97→
    98→**Ray.Toolkit.Automerge.FFI**
    99→
   100→The low-level FFI bindings to the Rust implementation. You typically don't interact with this directly.
   101→
   102→# Next Steps
   103→
   104→Start with the getting started guide to install the library and create your first document.
   105→
   106→Then explore the core concepts to understand documents, containers, and the data model.
   107→
   108→Finally, check the specific guides for working with maps, lists, text, synchronization, and repository doc handles.

    32→# Your First Document
    33→
    34→Let's create a simple document that stores user profile information.
    35→
    36→## Creating a Document
    37→
    38→Start by creating a new Automerge document:
    39→
    40→```csharp
    41→using Ray.Toolkit.Automerge;
    42→
    43→using var doc = AutomergeDocument.Create();
    44→```
    45→
    46→The document implements `IDisposable`. Use a `using` statement to ensure proper cleanup of native resources.
    47→
    48→## Getting the Root Object
    49→
    50→Every document has a root object where you store data:
    51→
    52→```csharp
    53→var root = doc.RootId;
    54→```
    55→
    56→The root is a Map container. You can add key-value pairs to it.
    57→
    58→## Adding Data
    59→
    60→Add different types of data to the root map:
    61→
    62→```csharp
    63→doc.PutString(root, "username", "alice");
    64→doc.PutInt64(root, "age", 30);
    65→doc.PutBoolean(root, "is_active", true);
    66→doc.PutTimestamp(root, "created_at", DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds());
    67→```

    69→The library supports multiple data types:
    70→- Strings
    71→- Integers (Int64, UInt64)
    72→- Floating-point numbers (Double)
    73→- Booleans
    74→- Timestamps (Unix milliseconds)
    75→- Bytes
    76→- Null values
    77→- Counters (CRDT counters)
    78→- Nested containers (Map, List, Text)
    79→
    80→## Committing Changes
    81→
    82→Changes remain pending until you commit them:
    83→
    84→```csharp
    85→var commitHash = doc.Commit("Add user profile");
    86→```
    87→
    88→The commit message helps track what changed. The method returns a hash identifying this commit.
    89→
    90→Automerge tracks all changes. You can roll back uncommitted changes using `doc.Rollback()`.
    91→
    92→## Viewing the Data
    93→
    94→Convert the document to JSON to see the current state:
    95→
    96→```csharp
    97→var json = doc.HydrateJson();
    98→Console.WriteLine(json);
    99→```
   100→
   101→This outputs something like:
   102→
   103→```json
   104→{
   105→  "username": "alice",
   106→  "age": 30,
   107→  "is_active": true,
   108→  "created_at": 1234567890
   109→}
   110→```
   111→
   112→# Complete Example
   113→
   114→Here's a complete program that creates a user profile:
   115→
   116→```csharp
   117→using System;
   118→using Ray.Toolkit.Automerge;
   119→
   120→using var doc = AutomergeDocument.Create();
   121→var root = doc.RootId;
   122→
   123→// Add user data
   124→doc.PutString(root, "username", "alice");
   125→doc.PutString(root, "email", "alice@example.com");
   126→doc.PutInt64(root, "age", 30);
   127→doc.PutBoolean(root, "email_verified", true);
   128→doc.PutTimestamp(root, "joined_at", DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds());
   129→
   130→// Create a nested preferences object
   131→var preferences = doc.PutObject(root, "preferences", AutomergeContainerType.Map);
   132→doc.PutString(preferences, "theme", "dark");
   133→doc.PutBoolean(preferences, "notifications", true);
   134→
   135→// Commit the changes
   136→var hash = doc.Commit("Create user profile");
   137→Console.WriteLine($"Committed: {hash}");
   138→
   139→// View the result
   140→var json = doc.HydrateJson();
   141→Console.WriteLine(json);
   142→
   143→// Check document state
   144→Console.WriteLine($"Actor ID: {doc.ActorId}");
   145→Console.WriteLine($"Pending operations: {doc.PendingOperations}");
   146→```
   147→
   148→# Understanding Actor IDs
   149→
   150→Each document has an actor ID that uniquely identifies who made changes:
   151→
   152→```csharp
   153→var actorId = doc.ActorId;
   154→Console.WriteLine($"This document's actor: {actorId}");
   155→```
   156→
   157→Automerge generates a random actor ID automatically. You can set a custom actor ID:
   158→
   159→```csharp
   160→doc.ActorId = "user-alice-device-1";
   161→```
   162→
   163→Actor IDs become important when syncing documents. They help Automerge track which peer made which changes.
   164→
   165→# Working with Nested Structures
   166→
   167→You can create nested maps and lists:
   168→
   169→```csharp
   170→using var doc = AutomergeDocument.Create();
   171→var root = doc.RootId;
   172→
   173→// Create a list of tags
   174→var tags = doc.PutObject(root, "tags", AutomergeContainerType.List);
   175→doc.ListInsertString(tags, 0, "developer");
   176→doc.ListInsertString(tags, 1, "golang");
   177→doc.ListInsertString(tags, 2, "rust");
   178→
   179→// Create a nested map for address
   180→var address = doc.PutObject(root, "address", AutomergeContainerType.Map);
   181→doc.PutString(address, "city", "San Francisco");
   182→doc.PutString(address, "country", "USA");
   183→
   184→doc.Commit("Add tags and address");
   185→
   186→var json = doc.HydrateJson();
   187→Console.WriteLine(json);
   188→```
   189→
   190→This creates a structure like:
   191→
   192→```json
   193→{
   194→  "tags": ["developer", "golang", "rust"],
   195→  "address": {
   196→    "city": "San Francisco",
   197→    "country": "USA"
   198→  }
   199→}
   200→```

     3→description: Understanding documents, actors, container types, and the Automerge data model
     4→---
     5→
     6→# Overview
     7→
     8→This guide explains the fundamental concepts behind Ray.Toolkit.Automerge.
     9→
    10→Understanding these concepts helps you design effective collaborative applications.
    11→
    12→# Documents
    13→
    14→An Automerge document is a container for your data. It tracks all changes made to that data over time.
    15→
    16→## Creating Documents
    17→
    18→You create a document using the static factory method:
    19→
    20→```csharp
    21→using var doc = AutomergeDocument.Create();
    22→```
    23→
    24→You can optionally specify an actor ID during creation:
    25→
    26→```csharp
    27→using var doc = AutomergeDocument.Create("user-alice-device-1");
    28→```
    29→
    30→## Document State
    31→
    32→Documents maintain several pieces of state:
    33→
    34→**Root Object** - Every document has a root map where you store top-level data.
    35→
    36→**Actor ID** - Identifies who is making changes to this document.
    37→
    38→**Pending Operations** - Changes you've made but haven't committed yet.
    39→
    40→**Commit History** - All committed changes with their messages and metadata.
    41→
    42→**Heads** - The latest commit hashes representing the current state.
    43→
    44→# Doc Handles
    45→
    46→When an Automerge document is managed by a repository you interact with it through a `DocHandle`. The handle serializes
    47→access, tracks locally generated change bytes, raises notifications, and exposes helpers for feeding remote updates back
    48→into the document. See the [Doc Handles](./doc-handles) guide for details on coordinating repository-backed documents.
    49→
    50→# Actors
    51→
    52→An actor represents a user or device making changes to a document.
    53→
    54→Each document has exactly one actor ID. When you sync documents, Automerge uses actor IDs to track who made which changes.
    55→
    56→## Actor ID Format
    57→
    58→Automerge generates random UUIDs as actor IDs by default:
    59→
    60→```csharp
    61→using var doc = AutomergeDocument.Create();
    62→Console.WriteLine(doc.ActorId); // Something like "a1b2c3d4..."
    63→```
    64→
    65→You can set custom actor IDs for easier debugging or tracking:
    66→
    67→```csharp
    68→doc.ActorId = "alice-laptop";
    69→```
    70→
    71→## Why Actor IDs Matter
    72→
    73→Actor IDs help resolve conflicts. When two actors make concurrent changes, Automerge uses the actor ID as a tiebreaker in some situations.
    74→
    75→They also help you track change provenance. You can see which actor made each modification.
    76→
    77→# Container Types
    78→
    79→Automerge provides three container types for organizing data:
    80→
    81→## Map
    82→
    83→Maps store key-value pairs, like a dictionary or object. The root of every document is a map.
    84→
    85→Use maps when you need named fields:
    86→
    87→```csharp
    88→var root = doc.RootId;
    89→doc.PutString(root, "username", "alice");
    90→doc.PutInt64(root, "score", 100);
    91→```
    92→
    93→Maps support any string as a key. Values can be any supported data type or nested container.
    94→
    95→## List
    96→
    97→Lists store ordered sequences of items, like an array.
    98→
    99→Use lists when order matters and you don't need named keys:
   100→
   101→```csharp
   102→var root = doc.RootId;
   103→var tasks = doc.PutObject(root, "tasks", AutomergeContainerType.List);
   104→doc.ListInsertString(tasks, 0, "Write documentation");
   105→doc.ListInsertString(tasks, 1, "Review code");
   106→```
   107→
   108→Lists support insertion at any index. Concurrent insertions from different actors maintain their relative order in predictable ways.
   109→
   110→## Text
   111→
   112→Text containers provide special CRDT semantics for collaborative text editing.
   113→
   114→Use text when multiple users might edit the same content simultaneously:
   115→
   116→```csharp
   117→var root = doc.RootId;
   118→var description = doc.PutObject(root, "description", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   119→doc.SpliceText(description, 0, 0, "Hello, world!");
   120→```
   121→
   122→Text containers track character-level operations. When two users edit nearby text, Automerge merges their changes intelligently.
   123→
   124→# Object IDs
   125→
   126→Every container in an Automerge document has a unique identifier called an Object ID.
   127→
   128→## Getting Object IDs
   129→
   130→When you create a container, you receive its Object ID:
   131→
   132→```csharp
   133→var root = doc.RootId; // The root map's ID
   134→var listId = doc.PutObject(root, "items", AutomergeContainerType.List); // New list's ID
   135→```
   136→
   137→You use these IDs to reference containers in subsequent operations:
   138→
   139→```csharp
   140→doc.ListInsertString(listId, 0, "first item");
   141→```
   142→
   143→## Object ID Lifetime
   144→
   145→Object IDs remain valid for the lifetime of the document. You can store them and use them later.
   146→
   147→However, they don't serialize to JSON. When you call `HydrateJson()`, you get the data values, not the internal Object IDs.
   148→
   149→# Commits
   150→
   151→Automerge uses an explicit commit model. Changes you make are pending until you commit them.
   152→
   153→## Creating Commits
   154→
   155→Call `Commit()` to finalize your changes:
   156→
   157→```csharp
   158→var hash = doc.Commit("Update user profile");
   159→```
   160→
   161→The method returns a commit hash. This hash uniquely identifies this set of changes.
   162→
   163→## Commit Messages
   164→
   165→Commit messages help you understand your change history:
   166→
   167→```csharp
   168→doc.Commit("Fix typo in description");
   169→doc.Commit("Add user preferences");
   170→doc.Commit("Update task priorities");
   171→```
   172→
   173→Messages are optional but recommended for debugging and auditing.
   174→
   175→## Commit Timestamps
   176→
   177→You can provide explicit timestamps:
   178→
   179→```csharp
   180→var timestamp = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds();
   181→doc.Commit("Scheduled update", timestamp);
   182→```
   183→
   184→Without an explicit timestamp, Automerge uses the current time.
   185→
   186→## Rollback
   187→
   188→You can discard uncommitted changes:
   189→
   190→```csharp
   191→doc.PutString(root, "temp", "temporary value");
   192→var count = doc.Rollback(); // Discards the PutString operation
   193→```
   194→
   195→The method returns the number of operations rolled back.
   196→
   197→# Conflict-Free Merging
   198→
   199→Automerge automatically merges concurrent changes without conflicts.
   200→
   201→## How It Works
   202→
   203→Each operation has a unique identifier combining the actor ID and a logical timestamp. When merging, Automerge uses these identifiers to determine operation order.
   204→
   205→Different data types have different merge semantics:
   206→
   207→**Last-Write-Wins** - For simple values like strings and numbers, the operation with the higher timestamp wins.
   208→
   209→**Addition** - For counters, values add together.
   210→
   211→**List Operations** - Insertions from different actors maintain their relative positions. Deletions apply regardless of other changes.
   212→
   213→**Text Operations** - Character insertions and deletions merge character by character.
   214→
   215→## Concurrent Edits Example
   216→
   217→Two users edit different fields in the same document:
   218→
   219→```csharp
   220→// Alice's document
   221→using var alice = AutomergeDocument.Create();
   222→var aliceRoot = alice.RootId;
   223→alice.PutString(aliceRoot, "title", "Project Plan");
   224→alice.Commit("Alice: Add title");
   225→
   226→// Bob's document (starts empty)
   227→using var bob = AutomergeDocument.Create();
   228→var bobRoot = bob.RootId;
   229→bob.PutString(bobRoot, "author", "Bob");
   230→bob.Commit("Bob: Add author");
   231→
   232→// Sync them
   233→var heads = alice.GetHeads();
   234→var changes = bob.GetChanges(heads);
   235→alice.ApplyChanges(changes);
   236→
   237→// Alice's document now has both title and author
   238→```
   239→
   240→Both changes survive the merge because they modify different keys.
   241→
   242→## Concurrent Updates to Same Key
   243→
   244→When two actors update the same key, the later timestamp wins:
   245→
   246→```csharp
   247→// Both Alice and Bob update "status" at roughly the same time
   248→alice.PutString(aliceRoot, "status", "in-progress");
   249→bob.PutString(bobRoot, "status", "completed");
   250→
   251→// After sync, one value wins based on timestamps and actor IDs
   252→```
   253→
   254→This is last-write-wins semantics. If you need different behavior, use counters or separate keys.
   255→
   256→# Data Types
   257→
   258→Automerge supports these primitive data types:
   259→
   260→**String** - UTF-8 text values.
   261→
   262→**Int64** - Signed 64-bit integers.
   263→
   264→**UInt64** - Unsigned 64-bit integers.
   265→
   266→**Double** - 64-bit floating-point numbers.
   267→
   268→**Boolean** - True or false values.
   269→
   270→**Timestamp** - Unix timestamps in milliseconds.
   271→
   272→**Bytes** - Binary data.
   273→
   274→**Null** - Explicit null values.
   275→
   276→**Counter** - CRDT counters that add together during merges.
   277→
   278→You can also use three container types (Map, List, Text) to create nested structures.
   279→
   280→# Change Tracking
   281→
   282→Automerge tracks every change with full history.
   283→
   284→## Getting Heads
   285→
   286→Heads represent the latest state:
   287→
   288→```csharp
   289→var heads = doc.GetHeads();
   290→foreach (var head in heads)
   291→{
   292→    Console.WriteLine($"Head: {head}");
   293→}
   294→```
   295→
   296→Most documents have one head. Multiple heads appear temporarily during merges.
   297→
   298→## Getting Changes
   299→
   300→Retrieve all changes since a known state:
   301→
   302→```csharp
   303→var knownHeads = new[] { "abc123...", "def456..." };
   304→var changes = doc.GetChanges(knownHeads);
   305→```
   306→
   307→This returns a list of binary change objects. You can send these to other peers for synchronization.
   308→
   309→## Last Local Change
   310→
   311→Get the most recent change made by this actor:
   312→
   313→```csharp
   314→var lastChange = doc.GetLastLocalChange();
   315→if (lastChange != null)
   316→{
   317→    Console.WriteLine($"Last change size: {lastChange.Length} bytes");
   318→}
   319→```
   320→
   321→This helps implement efficient change notification systems.
   322→
   323→# Document Lifecycle
   324→
   325→## Creation
   326→
   327→Start with a new document:
   328→
   329→```csharp
   330→using var doc = AutomergeDocument.Create();
   331→```
   332→
   333→## Modification
   334→
   335→Make changes and commit them:
   336→
   337→```csharp
   338→var root = doc.RootId;
   339→doc.PutString(root, "field", "value");
   340→doc.Commit("Update field");
   341→```
   342→
   343→## Synchronization
   344→
   345→Exchange changes with other documents:
   346→
   347→```csharp
   348→var changes = doc.GetChanges(otherDoc.GetHeads());
   349→otherDoc.ApplyChanges(changes);
   350→```
   351→
   352→## Persistence
   353→
   354→Save the document to bytes:
   355→
   356→```csharp
   357→var bytes = doc.Save();
   358→```
   359→
   360→Load it back later:
   361→
   362→```csharp
   363→using var restored = AutomergeDocument.Load(bytes);
   364→```
   365→
   366→## Cleanup
   367→
   368→Dispose of documents when done:
   369→
   370→```csharp
   371→doc.Dispose();
   372→```
   373→
   374→Or use a `using` statement for automatic disposal.
   375→
   376→# Performance Considerations
   377→
   378→## Commit Frequency
   379→
   380→Each commit adds overhead. Batch related changes into single commits:
   381→
   382→```csharp
   383→// Good: One commit for related changes
   384→doc.PutString(root, "first_name", "Alice");
   385→doc.PutString(root, "last_name", "Smith");
   386→doc.PutString(root, "email", "alice@example.com");
   387→doc.Commit("Update user info");
   388→
   389→// Less efficient: Many small commits
   390→doc.PutString(root, "first_name", "Alice");
   391→doc.Commit("Update first name");
   392→doc.PutString(root, "last_name", "Smith");
   393→doc.Commit("Update last name");
   394→```
   395→
   396→## Document Size
   397→
   398→Large documents take longer to serialize and sync. Consider splitting very large datasets into multiple documents.
   399→
   400→## Memory Management
   401→
   402→Documents hold native resources. Always dispose of them:
   403→
   404→```csharp
   405→using var doc = AutomergeDocument.Create();
   406→// Use the document
   407→// Automatic disposal happens here
   408→```
   409→

   421→

     2→title: Working with Text
     3→description: Learn how to use text containers for collaborative text editing in Automerge documents
     4→---
     5→
     6→# Overview
     7→
     8→Text containers provide special CRDT semantics designed for collaborative text editing.
     9→
    10→Unlike regular strings, text containers track character-level operations. This enables intelligent merging when multiple users edit the same content simultaneously.
    11→
    12→# Creating Text Containers
    13→
    14→Create a text container using `PutObject` with the Text container type:
    15→
    16→```csharp
    17→using var doc = AutomergeDocument.Create();
    18→var root = doc.RootId;
    19→
    20→var description = doc.PutObject(root, "description", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
    21→```
    22→
    23→This creates an empty text container stored under the "description" key.
    24→
    25→# Adding Text
    26→
    27→Use `SpliceText` to insert text at any position:
    28→
    29→```csharp
    30→var description = doc.PutObject(root, "description", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
    31→
    32→// Insert at the beginning (index 0)
    33→doc.SpliceText(description, 0, 0, "Hello, world!");
    34→doc.Commit("Add initial text");
    35→```
    36→
    37→The `SpliceText` method takes three parameters:
    38→- **Index**: Where to start the operation (0 = beginning)
    39→- **Delete count**: How many characters to delete
    40→- **Text**: The text to insert
    41→
    42→# Editing Text
    43→
    44→## Inserting Text
    45→
    46→Insert text at any position:
    47→
    48→```csharp
    49→var text = doc.PutObject(root, "content", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
    50→
    51→doc.SpliceText(text, 0, 0, "Hello, world!");
    52→doc.Commit("Initial text");
    53→
    54→// Insert at the beginning
    55→doc.SpliceText(text, 0, 0, "Greeting: ");
    56→doc.Commit("Add prefix");
    57→// Result: "Greeting: Hello, world!"
    58→
    59→// Insert in the middle (after "Greeting: Hello")
    60→doc.SpliceText(text, 16, 0, " beautiful");
    61→doc.Commit("Add adjective");
    62→// Result: "Greeting: Hello, beautiful world!"
    63→
    64→// Insert at the end
    65→doc.SpliceText(text, 33, 0, " How are you?");
    66→doc.Commit("Add question");
    67→// Result: "Greeting: Hello, beautiful world! How are you?"
    68→```
    69→
    70→## Deleting Text
    71→
    72→Delete characters by specifying a delete count:
    73→
    74→```csharp
    75→var text = doc.PutObject(root, "content", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
    76→
    77→doc.SpliceText(text, 0, 0, "Hello, wonderful world!");
    78→doc.Commit("Initial text");
    79→
    80→// Delete "wonderful " (10 characters starting at index 7)
    81→doc.SpliceText(text, 7, 10, "");
    82→doc.Commit("Remove adjective");
    83→// Result: "Hello, world!"
    84→```
    85→
    86→The empty string in the third parameter means "don't insert anything."
    87→
    88→## Replacing Text
    89→
    90→Replace text by deleting and inserting in one operation:
    91→
    92→```csharp
    93→var text = doc.PutObject(root, "greeting", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
    94→
    95→doc.SpliceText(text, 0, 0, "Hello, world!");
    96→doc.Commit("Initial");
    97→
    98→// Replace "world" (5 characters at index 7) with "everyone"
    99→doc.SpliceText(text, 7, 5, "everyone");
   100→doc.Commit("Change greeting");
   101→// Result: "Hello, everyone!"
   102→```
   103→
   104→This deletes 5 characters starting at index 7 and inserts "everyone" at that position.
   105→
   106→# Reading Text
   107→
   108→Use `HydrateJson` to get the text content as JSON:
   109→
   110→```csharp
   111→var text = doc.PutObject(root, "content", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   112→doc.SpliceText(text, 0, 0, "This is the text content.");
   113→doc.Commit("Add text");
   114→
   115→var json = doc.HydrateJson();
   116→using var parsed = JsonDocument.Parse(json);
   117→var content = parsed.RootElement.GetProperty("content").GetString();
   118→
   119→Console.WriteLine($"Content: {content}");
   120→// Output: Content: This is the text content.
   121→```
   122→
   123→Text containers serialize to regular strings in JSON.
   124→
   125→# Complete Example
   126→
   127→Here's a document editor simulation:
   128→
   129→```csharp
   130→using System;
   131→using System.Text.Json;
   132→using Ray.Toolkit.Automerge;
   133→
   134→using var doc = AutomergeDocument.Create();
   135→var root = doc.RootId;
   136→
   137→// Create a document with title and body
   138→doc.PutString(root, "title", "Meeting Notes");
   139→var body = doc.PutObject(root, "body", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   140→
   141→// Write initial content
   142→doc.SpliceText(body, 0, 0, "Meeting Date: 2024-01-15\n\n");
   143→doc.SpliceText(body, 26, 0, "Attendees:\n- Alice\n- Bob\n\n");
   144→doc.SpliceText(body, 52, 0, "Topics Discussed:\n");
   145→doc.Commit("Initial draft");
   146→
   147→// Add first topic
   148→doc.SpliceText(body, 70, 0, "1. Project timeline review\n");
   149→doc.Commit("Add first topic");
   150→
   151→// Add second topic
   152→doc.SpliceText(body, 97, 0, "2. Budget approval\n");
   153→doc.Commit("Add second topic");
   154→
   155→// Add notes to first topic
   156→var insertPos = 97; // Right before "2. Budget approval"
   157→doc.SpliceText(body, insertPos, 0, "   - Deadline confirmed for March 1\n   - All milestones on track\n\n");
   158→doc.Commit("Add timeline notes");
   159→
   160→// Fix typo in date

   191→# Collaborative Editing
   192→
   193→Text containers shine when multiple users edit simultaneously.
   194→
   195→## Non-Overlapping Edits
   196→
   197→When users edit different parts of the text, both changes apply:
   198→
   199→```csharp
   200→// Alice's document
   201→using var alice = AutomergeDocument.Create();
   202→var aliceRoot = alice.RootId;
   203→var aliceText = alice.PutObject(aliceRoot, "doc", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   204→alice.SpliceText(aliceText, 0, 0, "Hello, world!");
   205→alice.Commit("Alice: Initial");
   206→
   207→// Bob gets Alice's version
   208→var aliceChanges = alice.GetChanges(new string[0]);
   209→var bob = AutomergeDocument.Create();
   210→bob.ApplyChanges(aliceChanges);
   211→var bobRoot = bob.RootId;
   212→var bobText = bob.PutObject(bobRoot, "doc", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   213→
   214→// Alice adds prefix
   215→alice.SpliceText(aliceText, 0, 0, "Greeting: ");
   216→alice.Commit("Alice: Add prefix");
   217→// Alice's version: "Greeting: Hello, world!"
   218→
   219→// Bob adds suffix
   220→bob.SpliceText(bobText, 13, 0, " How are you?");
   221→bob.Commit("Bob: Add question");
   222→// Bob's version: "Hello, world! How are you?"
   223→
   224→// Sync
   225→var bobNewChanges = bob.GetChanges(alice.GetHeads());
   226→alice.ApplyChanges(bobNewChanges);
   227→
   228→// Result: "Greeting: Hello, world! How are you?"
   229→// Both edits appear in the merged version
   230→```

   232→## Nearby Edits
   233→
   234→When users edit near each other, Automerge merges intelligently:
   235→
   236→```csharp
   237→// Start with: "The quick fox"
   238→var alice = AutomergeDocument.Create();
   239→var aliceRoot = alice.RootId;
   240→var aliceText = alice.PutObject(aliceRoot, "text", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   241→alice.SpliceText(aliceText, 0, 0, "The quick fox");
   242→alice.Commit("Initial");
   243→
   244→// Bob gets the same starting point
   245→var aliceChanges = alice.GetChanges(new string[0]);
   246→var bob = AutomergeDocument.Create();
   247→bob.ApplyChanges(aliceChanges);
   248→var bobRoot = bob.RootId;
   249→var bobText = bob.PutObject(bobRoot, "text", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   250→
   251→// Alice adds "brown " after "quick "
   252→alice.SpliceText(aliceText, 10, 0, "brown ");
   253→alice.Commit("Alice: Add brown");
   254→// Alice's version: "The quick brown fox"
   255→
   256→// Bob adds "jumps" after "fox"
   257→bob.SpliceText(bobText, 13, 0, " jumps");
   258→bob.Commit("Bob: Add jumps");
   259→// Bob's version: "The quick fox jumps"
   260→
   261→// Sync
   262→var bobNewChanges = bob.GetChanges(alice.GetHeads());
   263→alice.ApplyChanges(bobNewChanges);
   264→
   265→// Result: "The quick brown fox jumps"
   266→// Both insertions preserved

   270→
   271→When both users delete text, Automerge applies both deletions:
   272→

   275→alice.SpliceText(aliceText, 4, 5, ""); // Delete first "very "
   276→// Alice's version: "The very quick fox"
   277→
   278→bob.SpliceText(bobText, 9, 5, ""); // Delete second "very "
   279→// Bob's version: "The very quick fox"

   282→// Both "very" instances removed

   285→# Text vs String
   286→
   287→Understanding when to use text containers versus regular strings:
   288→
   289→## Use Text Containers When:
   290→
   291→**Multiple users edit the same field**
   292→
   293→Text containers handle concurrent character-level edits:
   294→
   295→```csharp
   296→var description = doc.PutObject(root, "description", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   297→doc.SpliceText(description, 0, 0, "Product description goes here");
   298→```
   299→
   300→**You need fine-grained change tracking**
   301→
   302→Text containers track every character insertion and deletion.
   303→
   304→**Content is large or frequently edited**
   305→
   306→Text containers efficiently handle long documents with many edits.
   307→
   308→## Use Regular Strings When:
   309→
   310→**Only one user updates the field**
   311→
   312→Simple fields don't need text container complexity:
   313→
   314→```csharp
   315→doc.PutString(root, "username", "alice");
   316→doc.PutString(root, "email", "alice@example.com");
   317→```
   318→
   319→**Content replaces entirely**
   320→
   321→When you replace the whole value, use strings:
   322→
   323→```csharp
   324→doc.PutString(root, "status", "draft");
   325→// Later: completely replace
   326→doc.PutString(root, "status", "published");
   327→```
   328→
   329→**Values are short and static**
   330→
   331→Short identifiers or labels work fine as strings:
   332→
   333→```csharp
   334→doc.PutString(root, "id", "USER-12345");
   335→doc.PutString(root, "category", "documentation");
   336→```
   337→
   338→# Working with Text Length
   339→
   340→Calculate text length from the JSON representation:
   341→
   342→```csharp
   343→var text = doc.PutObject(root, "content", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   344→doc.SpliceText(text, 0, 0, "Hello, world!");
   345→doc.Commit("Add text");
   346→
   347→var json = doc.HydrateJson();
   348→using var parsed = JsonDocument.Parse(json);
   349→var content = parsed.RootElement.GetProperty("content").GetString();
   350→
   351→Console.WriteLine($"Length: {content.Length}"); // Length: 13
   352→```
   353→
   354→You need to hydrate to JSON to get the current text and its length.
   355→
   356→# Best Practices
   357→
   358→## Use Text for Collaborative Content
   359→
   360→Any field that multiple users might edit simultaneously should use text containers:
   361→
   362→```csharp
   363→// Good: Text for collaborative fields
   364→var description = doc.PutObject(root, "description", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   365→var notes = doc.PutObject(root, "notes", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   366→var comments = doc.PutObject(root, "comments", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   367→
   368→// Good: Strings for single-user fields
   369→doc.PutString(root, "created_by", "alice");
   370→doc.PutString(root, "id", "DOC-123");
   371→```
   372→
   373→## Calculate Positions Carefully
   374→
   375→Index positions matter for correct edits:
   376→
   377→```csharp
   378→// Current text: "Hello, world!"
   379→// To insert after "Hello, ": index 7
   380→doc.SpliceText(text, 7, 0, "beautiful ");
   381→
   382→// To replace "world": delete 5 chars at index 7, insert "everyone"
   383→doc.SpliceText(text, 7, 5, "everyone");
   384→```
   385→
   386→Wrong positions lead to incorrect edits. Hydrate the document to verify positions if needed.
   387→
   388→## Handle Empty Text
   389→
   390→Text containers can be empty initially:
   391→
   392→```csharp
   393→var text = doc.PutObject(root, "content", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   394→// Empty text container
   395→
   396→// Insert at index 0 to add content
   397→doc.SpliceText(text, 0, 0, "First content");
   398→```
   399→
   400→## Group Related Text Operations
   401→
   402→Batch multiple edits into one commit when they form a logical unit:
   403→
   404→```csharp
   405→// Good: Related edits in one commit
   406→doc.SpliceText(text, 0, 0, "# Title\n\n");
   407→doc.SpliceText(text, 9, 0, "This is the introduction.\n\n");
   408→doc.SpliceText(text, 36, 0, "## Section 1\n\n");
   409→doc.Commit("Add document structure");
   410→
   411→// Less efficient: Many small commits
   412→doc.SpliceText(text, 0, 0, "# Title\n\n");
   413→doc.Commit("Add title");
   414→doc.SpliceText(text, 9, 0, "This is the introduction.\n\n");
   415→doc.Commit("Add intro");
   416→```
   417→
   418→## Consider Line-Based Editing
   419→
   420→For structured content, consider organizing by lines:
   421→
   422→```csharp
   423→var content = doc.PutObject(root, "content", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   424→
   425→// Add line by line
   426→doc.SpliceText(content, 0, 0, "Line 1: Introduction\n");
   427→doc.SpliceText(content, 21, 0, "Line 2: Background\n");
   428→doc.SpliceText(content, 40, 0, "Line 3: Conclusion\n");
   429→doc.Commit("Add document lines");
   430→```
   431→
   432→This can make position calculations easier and supports line-based diffing.
   433→
   434→# Unicode and Special Characters
   435→
   436→Text containers handle UTF-8 encoding:
   437→
   438→```csharp
   439→var text = doc.PutObject(root, "content", AutomergeContainerType.Text);
   440→
   441→// Unicode characters work correctly
   442→doc.SpliceText(text, 0, 0, "Hello 👋 World 🌍!");
   443→doc.SpliceText(text, 18, 0, " Multiple languages: Bonjour, こんにちは, مرحبا");
   444→
   445→doc.Commit("Add international text");
   446→```
   447→
   448→Be aware that emoji and multi-byte characters count as their byte length, not as single characters. Calculate positions based on byte offsets.
   449→
   450→# Next Steps
   451→
   452→**Synchronization** - Learn how to sync text edits between multiple users.
   453→
   454→**Persistence** - Understand saving and loading documents with text containers.
   455→
   456→**Working with Lists** - Compare text containers with list-based approaches.
   457→
   458→**Working with Maps** - Learn when to use maps versus text containers.

     2→title: Doc Handles
     3→description: Manage repository-backed Automerge documents and coordinate local versus remote changes
     4→---
     5→
     6→# Overview
     7→
     8→`DocHandle` encapsulates an Automerge document that lives inside a repository. It provides a single coordination point for
     9→reading, mutating, and synchronizing document state while keeping track of locally generated changes that still need to
    10→be sent to peers.
    11→
    12→Unlike working with `AutomergeDocument` directly, a handle enforces serialized access, emits change notifications, and
    13→exposes helper utilities that a repository can use to drive networking or persistence.
    14→
    15→# Creating Handles
    16→
    17→When you ask a repository for a document (or create a new one), it returns a `DocHandle`. Handles can also be instantiated
    18→manually when wiring together prototypes or tests:
    19→
    20→```csharp
    21→using Ray.Automerge;
    22→using Ray.Toolkit.Automerge.Repository;
    23→
    24→// backing Automerge document
    25→var document = AutomergeDocument.Create("client-alice");
    26→
    27→// attach it to a handle
    28→var options = new DocHandleOptions<AutomergeDocument> { IsNew = true };
    29→using var handle = new DocHandle<AutomergeDocument>("tasks/alice", options, document);
    30→```
    31→
    32→A handle only becomes usable once the underlying document is attached. If you construct it without a document, call
    33→`Initialize` later:
    34→
    35→```csharp
    36→var handle = new DocHandle<AutomergeDocument>("tasks/alice");
    37→// ...load an AutomergeDocument from disk...
    38→handle.Initialize(loadedDocument, isNewDocument: false);
    39→```
    40→
    41→Use `WaitForDocumentAsync` or subscribe to `Ready` if you need to suspend work until the document is available.
    42→
    43→# Applying Local Changes
    44→
    45→`ChangeAsync` wraps mutations in a critical section, commits them, and records the generated Automerge change bytes so
    46→they can be forwarded to connected peers:
    47→
    48→```csharp
    49→var change = await handle.ChangeAsync(doc =>
    50→{
    51→  var root = doc.RootId;
    52→  doc.PutString(root, "title", "Daily notes");
    53→  doc.PutBoolean(root, "pinned", true);
    54→}, message: "pin daily note");
    55→
    56→if (change != null)
    57→{
    58→  // send to the sync layer
    59→  var pending = handle.DrainLocalChanges();
    60→  await transport.BroadcastAsync(handle.DocumentId, pending);
    61→}
    62→```
    63→
    64→If the mutation produces no observable difference (for example, setting a property to the same value), the method
    65→returns `null` and no change bytes are queued.
    66→
    67→# Processing Remote Updates
    68→
    69→Repositories use `ApplyRemoteChangesAsync` to apply change batches received from peers. The handle updates its cached
    70→heads and raises a `Changed` event so subscribers can refresh UI or trigger follow-up work:
    71→
    72→```csharp
    73→handle.Changed += (_, args) =>
    74→{
    75→  if (!args.IsLocal)
    76→  {
    77→    logger.LogInformation("Applied {Count} remote changes", args.AppliedChanges?.Count ?? 0);
    78→  }
    79→};
    80→
    81→await handle.ApplyRemoteChangesAsync(remoteChanges);
    82→```
    83→
    84→`ApplyRemoteChangesAsync` clones the supplied byte arrays before forwarding them to Automerge. You can safely reuse
    85→buffers after the method returns.
    86→
    87→# Reading Document State
    88→
    89→Handles expose `ReadAsync` helpers to perform synchronous reads while holding the internal lock:
    90→
    91→```csharp
    92→var json = await handle.ReadAsync(doc => doc.HydrateJson());
    93→var heads = handle.Heads;
    94→```
    95→
    96→Read delegates should avoid mutating the document—use `ChangeAsync` for writes so that change metadata stays consistent.
    97→
    98→# Direct Document Access
    99→
   100→When you need the underlying `AutomergeDocument`, call `Doc()` after the handle becomes ready:
   101→
   102→```csharp
   103→await handle.WhenReadyAsync();
   104→var doc = handle.Doc();            // throws if not ready
   105→var sameDoc = handle.DocSync();    // equivalent to Doc(), mirrors TS docSync()
   106→```
   107→
   108→The returned document is the live instance managed by the handle. Prefer `Change`/`ChangeAsync` for mutations so the
   109→handle can emit events and track local changes appropriately.
   110→
   111→Both synchronous and asynchronous change helpers are available:
   112→
   113→```csharp
   114→handle.Change(doc =>
   115→{
   116→  var root = doc.RootId;
   117→  doc.PutString(root, "title", "Hello");
   118→});
   119→
   120→await handle.ChangeAsync(doc =>
   121→{
   122→  var root = doc.RootId;
   123→  doc.PutBoolean(root, "pinned", true);
   124→});
   125→```
   126→
   127→# Typed Views
   128→
   129→`DocHandle<T>` is generic so you can project the underlying document into any shape you like. Supply a
   130→`DocHandleOptions<T>.ViewFactory` when constructing the handle and `Doc()` returns the projected value:
   131→
   132→```csharp
   133→var notesHandle = new DocHandle<NoteDto>(
   134→  "notes/123",
   135→  new DocHandleOptions<NoteDto>
   136→  {
   137→    ViewFactory = doc =>
   138→    {
   139→      var json = doc.HydrateJson();
   140→      return JsonSerializer.Deserialize<NoteDto>(json)!;
   141→    }
   142→  },
   143→  document);
   144→
   145→var note = await notesHandle.DocAsync();
   146→```
   147→
   148→# Events
   149→
   150→The C# port exposes the same event surface as the TypeScript handle. Subscribe to `Ready`, `Changed`, and
   151→`HeadsChanged` to react to document lifecycle events:
   152→
   153→```csharp
   154→handle.Ready += (_, args) =>
   155→{
   156→  logger.LogInformation("Handle {Id} ready (new: {IsNew})", args.Handle.DocumentId, args.IsNew);
   157→};
   158→
   159→handle.Changed += (_, args) =>
   160→{
   161→  if (args.IsLocal)
   162→  {
   163→    syncQueue.Enqueue(args.LocalChange!.Changes);
   164→  }
   165→};
   166→
   167→handle.HeadsChanged += (_, args) =>
   168→{
   169→  cache.Store(args.Heads);
   170→};
   171→```
   172→
   173→# Disposal and Safety Guarantees
   174→
   175→Disposing a handle also disposes the underlying `AutomergeDocument`. All future operations throw `ObjectDisposedException`.
   176→This prevents background tasks from publishing stale changes after a repository shuts down:
   177→
   178→```csharp
   179→handle.Dispose();
   180→await Assert.ThrowsAsync<ObjectDisposedException>(() => handle.ChangeAsync(_ => { }));
   181→```
   182→
   183→Because the handle serializes access with a semaphore and forces callers through the provided API surface, repositories
   184→can independently drain `DrainLocalChanges`, listen for `Changed`, and orchestrate persistence without worrying about
   185→concurrent writes or missed change batches.
